title: Aspectual Se: Doing Something All the Way Through

sections.content: In everyday Spanish, verbs of consuming, learning and perceiving — *comerse*, *beberse*, *tomarse*, *leerse*, *aprenderse*, *saberse*, *fumarse* — often take a pronoun (*me, te, se, nos, se*) to mark **completeness**: the action is carried out to the very end on a whole, definite or quantified object (*Se comió el pastel entero*, *Me leí el libro de una sentada*, *Se sabe todos los nombres de memoria*). This *se* is neither reflexive (nobody eats himself) nor passive. Without a definite or quantified object, aspectual *se* sounds odd: you say *Comió pan* (some bread), not *Se comió pan*, whereas *Se comió todo el pan* is completely natural. It is very common in speech across all varieties of Spanish and less usual in formal writing.

sections.title: Plain verb vs aspectual se
rows: *Se comió el pastel entero*, *Se bebió el jugo de un trago*, *Me leí el capítulo en diez minutos*.
*Se aprendió el discurso de memoria*, *Nos sabemos todas las canciones*.
*Se comió el bocado* means 'he ate the whole bite up', not 'he ate himself'.

items.spanish: Se comió el pastel entero sin dejar ni un bocado.
items.english: He ate the whole cake without leaving a single bite.

items.spanish: Tenía tanta sed que se bebió el vaso de agua de un trago.
items.english: She was so thirsty that she drank the glass of water in one gulp.

items.spanish: Me leí la novela entera de una sentada el domingo pasado.
items.english: I read the whole novel in one sitting last Sunday.

items.spanish: Se sabe de memoria todos los pasos de la receta.
items.english: She knows all the steps of the recipe by heart.

sections.content: English marks this completeness with particles like *up* (*eat up*, *drink up*) or *all the way through*. Never attach aspectual *se* to a bare, unquantified noun (*Se bebió agua* for 'she drank some water' sounds wrong): either add a definite/quantified object (*Se bebió un vaso de agua*) or drop *se* (*Bebió agua*).
